clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant focal palmoplantar keratoderma (tylosis) associated with a very high lifetime risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma
The keratoderma is typically focal and pressure-related, affecting the soles more than the palms, often with onset in later childhood
Oral leucokeratosis (white oral mucosal thickening) may accompany the palmoplantar disease
Caused by dominant mutations in RHBDF2 encoding the inactive rhomboid protease iRhom2
The oesophageal cancer risk is the dominant clinical concern and warrants endoscopic surveillance from adulthood
A detailed family history is essential, as the malignancy risk clusters in affected kindreds
Management combines emollients/keratolytics for the skin with lifelong cancer surveillance and prompt investigation of oesophageal symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Howel-Evans syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by gain-of-function mutations in RHBDF2, which encodes iRhom2, a regulator of the enzyme ADAM17 (TACE). ADAM17 controls the shedding and signalling of epidermal growth factor receptor ligands, so the mutations enhance EGFR-pathway signalling and epithelial proliferation. In the palmoplantar epidermis this drives the focal hyperkeratosis (tylosis), while in the oesophageal squamous epithelium the same dysregulated proliferative signalling and impaired wound-healing response markedly increase susceptibility to squamous cell carcinoma. The heightened, lifelong malignancy risk is the defining pathophysiological feature.
additionalDifferentials: Other focal or diffuse hereditary palmoplantar keratodermas without cancer association
Keratoderma associated with internal malignancy (paraneoplastic acrokeratosis)
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for surveillance and evaluation of symptoms
Skin biopsy of palmoplantar lesions where the diagnosis is uncertain
Examination of the oral mucosa for leucokeratosis
Detailed pedigree and family cancer history
Referral for genetic counselling of at-risk relatives
redFlags: Dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss or new gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting oesophageal carcinoma
Change in an area of oral leucokeratosis
A strong family history of oesophageal cancer prompting urgent surveillance
reference.prognosis: The keratoderma itself is benign, but the lifetime risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma is very high and is the main determinant of prognosis. Outcome depends heavily on early detection through surveillance, since oesophageal cancer diagnosed late carries a poor prognosis.
pitfalls: Treating the keratoderma as an isolated skin problem and failing to institute oesophageal cancer surveillance
Dismissing new swallowing symptoms in an affected individual
Not offering genetic testing and counselling to relatives at risk
Confusing it with common non-syndromic keratodermas that carry no malignancy risk
management: Treat the palmoplantar keratoderma symptomatically with emollients, keratolytics such as topical salicylic acid and urea, and mechanical paring, adding oral retinoids in severe disease
Institute lifelong upper gastrointestinal endoscopic surveillance from adulthood for early detection of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma
Promptly investigate dysphagia or new oesophageal symptoms with endoscopy and biopsy
Advise avoidance of additional oesophageal carcinogens, with smoking cessation and reduction of alcohol
Examine and manage oral leucokeratosis and provide podiatry for painful plantar lesions
Refer for clinical genetics with RHBDF2 testing, genetic counselling and surveillance enrolment of at-risk relatives
